sources.news_title: Armed Man Charges Amy Acton at Ohio Fair, Arrested
sources.text:
Armed man charged at Ohio gubernatorial candidate Amy Acton at Canfield Fair, police say
An armed man carrying two pistols and a taser forced his way through a crowd toward Democratic Ohio gubernatorial candidate Amy Acton at the Canfield Fair on Sunday, knocking over multiple people before state troopers stopped him, drawing bipartisan condemnation in a race already defined by sharp divisions.
Patrick M. Havas, 38, was intercepted by Ohio State Highway Patrol troopers after he charged toward Acton at the Mahoning County Democratic Party booth, Fox News reported. Havas knocked multiple fairgoers to the ground while trying to reach the candidate. Troopers found him carrying a taser and two pistols when they took him into custody.
Acton herself was not injured. But several campaign volunteers and bystanders were hurt after Havas barreled through the crowd. He was booked into Mahoning County Jail on two counts of assault and one count of disorderly conduct. Authorities noted that no weapons were brandished or removed from holsters during the incident.
Havas carried brass knuckles, two handguns, and a taser to a county fair
The full inventory of what Havas brought to the Canfield Fair raises serious questions about his intent. AP News reported that in addition to the taser and two pistols, authorities recovered a set of brass knuckles from Havas. That is not the loadout of a man who wandered into a political tent by accident.
No motive has been publicly stated. Law enforcement has not said whether Havas targeted Acton specifically or what prompted him to charge toward her. The charges filed, assault and disorderly conduct, are relatively modest given the arsenal he was carrying, and it remains unclear whether additional charges could follow.
The Acton campaign released a statement through communications director Addie Bullock shortly after the incident, as Breitbart reported:
"While attending the Canfield Fair, an armed individual lunged at Dr. Acton, injuring multiple people. Dr. Acton and Eric are grateful for the swift and decisive action of law enforcement and are praying for the recovery of those injured. This kind of violence has no place in Ohio. Dr. Acton will always stand up to the chaos, hate and vitriol that pits us against one another."
The identity of "Eric," referenced in the campaign statement alongside Acton, was not clarified. The severity of the injuries sustained by those knocked down has not been disclosed by local media or law enforcement.
Ramaswamy and DeWine both condemned the incident within hours
Acton's Republican opponent in the governor's race, Vivek Ramaswamy, responded quickly. His communications director, Connie Luck, released a statement that left no ambiguity:
"Candidates should be able to meet with voters without having to worry about threats or violence. What happened today is completely unacceptable and has no place in politics, and we hope no one was hurt."
Republican Gov. Mike DeWine also weighed in. The Washington Examiner reported DeWine's statement: "Violence or the threat of violence at political or public events is always unacceptable."
The bipartisan response was the right one. Whatever voters think of Amy Acton's politics, and conservatives in Ohio have plenty of reasons to oppose her candidacy on the merits, no candidate should face an armed assailant at a county fair. That principle is not partisan. It is foundational.
The incident fits a disturbing pattern of rising political hostility across the country. Newsmax noted that federal political committees spent more than $40 million on security during the 2023, 24 campaign cycle alone, reflecting the growing threat environment that candidates at every level now face.
That figure tells a story by itself. When campaigns have to divert tens of millions of dollars from voter outreach to personal protection, something has gone badly wrong in the country's political culture. The problem is not confined to one party or one ideology. The politically motivated murder of Minnesota House Speaker Melissa Hortman and her husband earlier this year was a grim reminder that political violence can strike anyone, anywhere.
County fairs should not require a security perimeter
The Canfield Fair is one of the largest and oldest county fairs in Ohio, the kind of event where candidates have pressed flesh and handed out flyers for generations. It is not a high-security venue. It is a place where families bring their kids to look at livestock and eat funnel cake.
That a man armed with two handguns, a taser, and brass knuckles could get close enough to a gubernatorial candidate to knock over multiple people before being stopped raises obvious questions about security protocols at open-air political events. Ohio State Highway Patrol troopers ultimately intervened, but the fact that Havas reached the Democratic Party booth while carrying that kind of hardware suggests gaps that need addressing.
The broader trend of threats against political figures, from both sides of the aisle, has reshaped how campaigns operate. Ohio's own political landscape has seen its share of turbulence in recent years, and the escalation from heated rhetoric to physical confrontation is a line that should concern every voter regardless of party.
Several key questions remain unanswered. Authorities have not disclosed a motive. They have not explained why Havas was carrying such a heavy arsenal to a county fair. And the charges currently filed, two misdemeanor-level assaults and disorderly conduct, may not reflect the full scope of what happened if investigators determine Havas had a specific plan.
Whether prosecutors upgrade those charges will say a lot about how seriously Ohio's justice system treats threats against candidates. Voters are watching. The coarsening of political confrontation has been a growing concern across the Midwest, and the gap between aggressive rhetoric and physical danger keeps narrowing.
Acton, a physician who previously served as Ohio's health director, is running to succeed DeWine in a race that has drawn national attention largely because of Ramaswamy's involvement. Whatever policy disagreements define that contest, and there are many, they belong in debates, town halls, and ballot boxes.
Not at the end of a man's fist in a fairground tent.
A republic that cannot protect its candidates from armed assailants at county fairs has a problem no election can fix. The response from both parties was correct on Sunday, but condemnation without consequence is just words. Prosecutors in Mahoning County now have the chance to show that Ohio takes this seriously.
When a man shows up to a political event carrying two pistols, a taser, and brass knuckles, the law should treat him like what he is, not like someone who got a little rowdy at the fair.

sources.news_title: Armed attacker arrested after lunging at Ohio Jewish gubernatorial candidate Amy Acton
sources.text:
Ohio gubernatorial candidate Amy Acton, a Jewish Democrat, was unharmed following an attack by an armed individual at the sprawling Canfield Fair on Sunday.
Police arrested 38-year-old Patrick Havas, who had pushed his way through a crowd in a Democratic Party fairgrounds tent where she was speaking, the Mahoning County Sheriff’s Office announced on Sunday evening.
“While attending the Canfield Fair, an armed individual lunged at Dr. Acton, injuring multiple people,” Addie Bullock, communications director for the Acton campaign, said in a statement.
“This kind of violence has no place in Ohio,” Bullock added. “Dr. Acton will always stand up to the chaos, hate and vitriol that pits us against one another.”
Acton, who would be Ohio’s first Jewish governor if elected, is a former director of the Ohio Department of Health and completed residencies in both pediatrics and preventative medicine.
Republican Vivek Ramaswamy, Acton’s opponent in the upcoming election, released a statement condemning the attack on Sunday. His communications director, Connie Luck, stressed that “candidates should be able to meet with voters without having to worry about threats or violence.”
“What happened today is completely unacceptable and has no place in politics, and we hope that no one was hurt,” she added.
Havas had at first entered the fairgrounds tent and began recording Acton’s speech on his cell phone, but when he began pushing, Ohio State Highway Patrol troopers confronted him, according to the sheriff’s office. During the confrontation, two people were knocked to the ground and Havas was taken into custody by Canfield Fair police.
Following Havas’s arrest, police said they found two handguns and a set of brass knuckles in his possession, although no weapons were ever brandished or removed from their holsters.
Detectives on Sunday night added that they’d be continuing the investigation and would be filing charges after consulting with the Mahoning County Prosecutor.
The Canfield Fair, established in 1846, describes itself as the third-largest county fair nationwide. The fairgrounds, located about 75 miles southeast of Cleveland, sits on 353 acres of land and houses more than 60 buildings.

sources.news_title: Acton back on campaign trail after incident where man allegedly lunged at her
sources.text:
Democratic nominee for Ohio governor Dr. Amy Acton was back on the campaign trail in Cleveland on Monday, less than 24 hours after officials said an armed man rushed toward her while she spoke to a crowd at the Canfield Fair near Youngstown.
According to the Mahoning County Sheriff's Office, Acton's Ohio State Highway Patrol security detail stopped Patrick Havas, 38, before he could reach her. Law enforcement said he was armed with two handguns and a set of brass knuckles but did not pull them out during the incident.
Havas was arrested and is currently in the Mahoning County jail. He faces assault and disorderly conduct charges. According to court records, Havas has a prior disorderly conduct conviction from 2008.
During a Cleveland Labor Day Parade event, which featured bolstered security according to WCPO-sister station News 5 Cleveland, Acton spoke about what happened on Sunday.
"Yes, we had a rough day yesterday. I am so thankful to our first responders, our state highway patrol and everyone who helped out the people who were injured," Acton said. "And our prayers are with them. I am a fierce warrior in this fight. That’s exactly why I’m running."
Acton's Democratic nominee for Ohio lieutenant governor, David Pepper, spoke to the media Monday about what happened inside the tent. He said he wasn't a witness to the incident.
"(Havas) very aggressively moved into a crowded tent, knocked some elderly folks over who were initially hurt, and to Amy's credit, she's got a sort of a first-responder mentality," he said. "Right after the incident, she actually went and helped take care of one of the people who was hurt."
Pepper said two people allegedly knocked down by Havas are doing fine and credited law enforcement with preventing a worse outcome.
"The state highway patrol, first responders, did an amazing job of stopping what was a scary incident," Pepper said.
Pepper said the campaign has been security-conscious from the start and will continue working with OSHP going forward.
"There's no room for this kind of violence, and, and some of the rhetoric that's leading to it is just out of control," Pepper said.
Republican gubernatorial candidate Vivek Ramaswamy, who said he was briefly at the Canfield Fair but learned of the incident afterward, condemned the incident Monday.
"The first and most important thing is I am very grateful that Dr. Acton and her family are doing well. That's the most important thing," Ramaswamy said. "Political violence has no place in America. Period. Full stop. The threat of political violence has no place in America. Full stop."
Ramaswamy also called for a debate with Acton, saying it would set an example for the public of how democracy is supposed to work.
University of Cincinnati political science professor David Niven said the incident reflects a shift in American politics.
"I think there's been an upswing in threats and attacks on governors and, and candidates for governor in the recent political era," he said. "Political violence was not invented in 2026, but what's different is just the ubiquity of it."
Niven said technology has made candidates easier to track, creating a tension between open campaigning and security.
"This is one of the unsolvable aspects of, of modern campaigns. It's far easier and faster to know where a candidate's going to be," Niven said. "They want that information out there. But on the other hand, for those with ill intent, it's never been easier to track a candidate"
The Mahoning County Sheriff's Office is still investigating the incident while OSHP investigates any potential threat assessment.
In a social media post over the weekend, Republican Sen. Jon Husted called what happened disturbing.
"We are grateful for law enforcement’s quick response," he wrote on X, formerly Twitter. "There is no place for this kind of behavior, and it must never be tolerated."
Husted's opponent for November, Democrat Sherrod Brown, thanked law enforcement in a separate post.
"Connie and I are grateful that Dr. Acton and all involved are safe, and we thank the Ohio law enforcement officers for their quick and professional response," he wrote.

sources.news_title: Armed man arrested after charging toward candidate for Ohio governor | Honolulu Star-Advertiser
sources.text:
Armed man arrested after charging toward candidate for Ohio governor
An armed man was arrested Sunday after forcing his way through a crowd toward Dr. Amy Acton, the Democratic nominee for Ohio governor, authorities said.
Acton was giving a speech at the Mahoning County Democratic Party tent at a fair in Canfield, in the northeastern part of the state, when a man pushed through the crowd, knocking over two elderly audience members, according to the county sheriff, Jerry Greene, and two witnesses. The man did not draw his weapons, according to Greene and the witnesses. Acton was not injured.
Two officers of the Ohio State Highway Patrol, part of Acton’s security detail, detained and handcuffed the man, according to Acton’s campaign and the sheriff.
The man was found to be carrying two pistols and a Taser in the shape of brass knuckles after he was detained, according to the sheriff and the Ohio State Highway Patrol. Ohio law allows residents to possess and carry concealed firearms without a permit.
The man, identified as 38-year-old Patrick Havas of Canfield, was booked into the county jail on one charge of disorderly conduct and two counts of misdemeanor assault, one for each individual he knocked over, authorities said. The victims were assessed for potential injuries and chose not to seek further treatment, Greene said.
The Ohio State Highway Patrol and the Mahoning County Sheriff’s Office are investigating the incident. Havas did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

A representative for Acton’s campaign said in a statement that a person who was armed “lunged at” Acton.
“Multiple people” were injured in the incident, according to the statement from Addie Bullock, communications director for Acton’s campaign. Bullock said Acton and her husband, Eric, were grateful for the “decisive action of law enforcement” and praying for those injured.
Asked about the man’s intent, the sheriff said: “I think it was to ask her a couple of questions. He was just, you know, pretty aggressive about it.”
John Boccieri, a former Democratic congressman who is running for the Ohio state House, said he witnessed the altercation. After the man was handcuffed, “he was screaming, ‘Dr. Acton, Dr. Acton,’” Boccieri said.
Mike Ray, a City Council member in Youngstown, who said he witnessed the incident, recalled hearing the same thing. He also said the man began “heckling” Acton as she was addressing the crowd, then knocked two older adults to the ground.
“It was surreal, turning and seeing this guy being drug away,” said Ray, who is also a member of the Ohio Democratic Party executive committee.
Gov. Mike DeWine, a Republican, said in a statement that the man tried to “forcefully push himself toward Dr. Acton,” and that he injured other attendees.
“We spoke to Dr. Acton this afternoon and she said to share with Ohioans that she is ok,” DeWine wrote in a post on the social platform X. “Violence or the threat of violence at political or public events is always unacceptable.”
Earlier in the day at the fair, Ramaswamy had visited and climbed in the back of a pickup truck to make a speech to around 200 people at the Republican tent. Acton and Ramaswamy are running in one of the country’s most competitive governor’s races.
Ramaswamy’s campaign issued a statement saying that what happened with Acton was “completely unacceptable.”
“Candidates should be able to meet with voters without having to worry about threats or violence,” Connie Luck, Ramaswamy’s spokesperson, said in a statement Sunday evening.
As the sun set in Canfield on Sunday evening, hundreds of people continued enjoying the fair as if nothing unusual had occurred. But at the Democratic Party tent, the hubbub of the day was still unfolding. Visitor after visitor stopped in to ask if what they had seen on social media and the local news was true.
“Now everybody wants Amy signs and Amy buttons,” said Bernadette Pernotto, a volunteer with the Mahoning County Democratic Party. Pernetto said she had been standing feet away from Acton when the suspect entered the tent. She said it was like watching bowling pins fall as he knocked down the two older people in his way.
Some fairgoers said the news made them hesitate about coming out Sunday night. Annika McCabe, 24, texted her friends to ask if they still wanted to go.
“It’s just a microcosm of how escalated things have become,” McCabe said. “But these things are going to keep happening, and we have to keep living our lives.”
At the Republican tent, Tom McCabe, chair of the Mahoning County Republican Party, said the incident was disturbing.
“Everyone is shocked that it happened in our hometown,” McCabe said.

sources.text:
WASHINGTON — An armed assailant charged toward the Democratic candidate for Ohio governor, Amy Acton, on Sunday during a campaign stop at the Canfield Fair, injuring several people before he was stopped by troopers, the Ohio State Highway Patrol said.
The Ohio State Highway Patrol said in a statement that a man it identified as Patrick Havas, 38, forced his way through a crowd, knocking over multiple members of the audience as he moved toward Acton, the state’s former public health director. He had a taser and two pistols, the statement said.
The Mahoning County Sheriff’s Office said two handguns and a set of brass knuckles were recovered after his arrest, and “no weapons were ever brandished or even removed from their holsters.”
Havas was taken to the county jail and booked on charges of disorderly conduct and two counts of assault, the highway patrol statement said, adding that no other details were available pending an investigation. Online court records didn’t yet list the case, and it wasn’t clear as of Sunday night whether Havas has an attorney.
Republican Gov. Mike DeWine said in a statement that the man “tried to forcefully push himself” toward Acton as she was speaking at the fair in Canfield, in northeastern Ohio. “Violence or the threat of violence at political or public events is always unacceptable,” he added.
The attempted attack is the latest political violence to roil the United States. And the Ohio gubernatorial race is one of the most high-profile races this year as the campaigns enter the final six weeks of campaigning before the election in November.
Acton is facing Republican Vivek Ramaswamy, who has parlayed his national name recognition, tech industry connections and alliance with President Donald Trump into a record fundraising haul that he is tapping for advertising spots aimed at the November election. He is using campaign rallies and advertising to criticize Acton.
Ramaswamy’s campaign called the incident Sunday unacceptable.
“Candidates should be able to meet with voters without having to worry about threats or violence. What happened today is completely unacceptable and has no place in politics, and we hope hope that no one was hurt,” Ramaswamy’s communications director, Connie Luck, said in a statement.
Addie Bullock, communications director for Acton’s campaign, said in a statement that the suspect “lunged” at Acton. She said the Democratic candidate “will always stand up to the chaos, hate and vitriol that pits us against one another.”
The incident brought condemnation from Ohio Republican Sen. Jon Husted, who said on X that he and his wife were “disturbed by the attempted attack on Amy Acton today at the Canfield Fair. We are grateful for law enforcement’s quick response. There is no place for this kind of behavior, and it must never be tolerated.”
The country has seen a rise in political violence over the past decade. That includes the 2017 shooting at a Republican congressional baseball team practice in Alexandria, Virginia; the 2022 hammer assault on the husband of Democratic then-House Speaker Nancy Pelosi in California; the 2024 assassination attempt on Donald Trump at a Pennsylvania rally during his presidential campaign as well as another on the president at this year’s White House Correspondents’ Association Dinner in April; and the assassinations last year of a Democratic Minnesota state lawmaker and her husband and of conservative commentator Charlie Kirk in Utah.
Federal political committees spent more than $40 million on expenses labeled as security during the 2023-24 campaign cycle, the most recent one for which data is publicly available, according a report released in April from the Public Service Alliance, a nonpartisan group that focuses on security for public officials.
Before running for governor, Acton was recruited by DeWine in 2019 to lead the Ohio Department of Health while serving as an associate professor of public health at Ohio State University. As the COVID-19 pandemic ramped up in early 2020, she was thrown into the state and national spotlight — becoming a source of comfort to many viewers of the governor’s daily news conferences.
For her service as health director, Acton earned the John F. Kennedy Library Foundation’s Profile in COVID Courage Award, the Columbus Foundation’s Spirit of Columbus Award and Ohio State’s highest alumni honor, the Alumni Medalist Award.
Her position as the face of the DeWine administration’s aggressive stance against the virus also earned Acton many enemies, among them Statehouse Republicans and average Ohioans who opposed pandemic restrictions.

sources.news_title: Ohio Man Charged with Assault After Lunging at Physician Amy Acton at Canfield Fair, Injuring Bystanders
sources.text:
Ohio Man Charged with Assault After Lunging at Physician Amy Acton at Canfield Fair, Injuring Bystanders
An armed 38-year-old Ohio man has been booked into the Mahoning County Jail on two counts of assault and one count of disorderly conduct after pushing through a crowd toward physician Amy Acton at the Canfield Fair, knocking two people to the ground. Acton, a doctor and Ohio's former state health director, was not injured and remained on-site to attend to one of the people who was hurt.
The Ohio State Highway Patrol, which provides Acton a protective detail because she is a candidate for governor, identified the man as Patrick Havas of Canfield. Troopers said he was carrying a Taser and two pistols. The Mahoning County Sheriff's Office said two handguns and a set of brass knuckles were recovered after the arrest, and that "no weapons were ever brandished or even removed from their holsters."
For readers outside Ohio, the health significance here is not the campaign. It is that a physician who ran a state health department during a pandemic required an armed protective detail at a county fair, and that this is no longer unusual in American public health.
The Confirmed Sequence at the Fairgrounds
The incident occurred around 2:30 p.m. Sunday at the annual Canfield Fair in Mahoning County, near Youngstown. Sheriff's office spokesperson Gerry Ricciutti said Havas entered the Mahoning County Democratic Party tent holding a cellphone as though recording, then began forcing his way through the crowd as Acton spoke.
Highway patrol troopers on her detail confronted him. Two audience members were knocked to the ground during that confrontation and were injured. Investigators said no weapon was displayed at any point.
Havas has been charged but not convicted, and the charges are allegations. Investigators have not established a motive, and officials said no further details were available while the investigation continues. Readers should treat any online claim about motive as unverified until law enforcement releases findings.
Ohio Attorney General Andy Wilson called the attempted violence unacceptable and expressed confidence in the highway patrol's protective work. Republican Gov. Mike DeWine, who appointed Acton to lead the Ohio Department of Health in 2019, said that "violence or the threat of violence at political or public events is always unacceptable."
A Pattern That Reshaped the Public Health Workforce
Acton's history makes this incident resonate beyond one fairground. She resigned as Ohio's health director in June 2020 after months of backlash over pandemic orders that included armed demonstrators outside her suburban Columbus home, antisemitic signage at protests, and a legislative effort to strip the health director's emergency authority.
That experience was widespread rather than isolated. Research published in the American Journal of Public Health documented 1,499 harassment reports across local health departments between March 2020 and January 2021, with 57 percent of the 583 departments that responded to the survey reporting harassment of leadership or staff. The same Johns Hopkins analysis identified 222 public health officials who left their positions during that period, 36 percent of whom reported harassment.
A separate analysis of a 2021 CDC survey of 26,174 state, tribal, local and territorial public health workers found that 12 percent had received job-related threats and 24 percent had been bullied or harassed, with 32 percent experiencing at least one form of workplace violence.
The Household Consequence of a Thinner Bench
Losing experienced health directors is not an abstract institutional problem. Local health departments run the systems families use without thinking about them: restaurant inspections, school immunization records, well water and beach testing, tuberculosis and sexually transmitted infection clinics, lead screening for children in older housing, and the contact tracing that contains a measles or hepatitis A exposure.
When a director with a decade of local knowledge leaves, and the position sits vacant or turns over repeatedly, response times lengthen, and institutional memory disappears. A department that has cycled through three leaders in five years is slower to recognize an unusual cluster of illness and slower to coordinate with hospitals and school districts when one appears.
That is the practical pathway from an incident at an Ohio fairground to a family in any American metro area. Parents in Columbus, Cleveland, Cincinnati or any other city rely on health department staff they will never meet. Recruiting and retaining those staff becomes harder when the job carries a credible expectation of harassment.
The effect is uneven. Large urban health departments have deeper staffing benches and can absorb turnover. Smaller county departments, which often operate with a handful of professional staff, cannot. Rural and small-metro counties are where a single departure changes what a department can actually deliver.
Where the Case Goes from Here
Havas faces two counts of assault and one count of disorderly conduct. Accounts of the degree of those assault charges have differed, with the sheriff's office describing them as misdemeanors while county jail records listed felony assault. The Ohio State Highway Patrol investigation remains open, and additional or amended charges are possible depending on what investigators find. Prosecutors in Mahoning County will determine how the case proceeds.
The injured bystanders' conditions have not been detailed publicly. Acton was reported to have remained on-site attending to one of them, though her campaign has not released clinical information about anyone hurt, and no hospital has issued a statement.
Readers should watch for the highway patrol's completed investigative findings, any prosecutorial filing in Mahoning County, and whether Ohio officials revisit protective arrangements for candidates and public officials at large open-air public events. MedicalDaily will follow developments in the case and any policy response affecting public health staff safety.
For now, the verified facts are narrow: a man carrying weapons pushed through a crowd toward a physician, two bystanders were hurt, no weapon was drawn, and charges have been filed. Everything about why remains under investigation.
Key Questions Answered
What happened at the Canfield Fair? An armed man pushed through a crowd toward physician Amy Acton as she spoke, knocking two audience members to the ground before troopers stopped him.
Was anyone seriously hurt? Two bystanders were injured. Acton was not hurt. Officials have not released details about the injured people's conditions.
What charges were filed? Two counts of assault and one count of disorderly conduct. The charges are allegations, and the investigation remains open.
Was a weapon used? No. The Mahoning County Sheriff's Office said no weapons were brandished or removed from their holsters. Two handguns, brass knuckles and a Taser were recovered.
Why is a health news outlet covering this? Acton is a physician and former state health director. Threats against public health officials are a documented workforce problem affecting local health departments nationwide.
How common is harassment of public health officials? Johns Hopkins researchers documented 1,499 harassment reports, affecting 57 percent of surveyed local health departments early in the pandemic, alongside 222 national position departures.
What happens next in the case? The Ohio State Highway Patrol investigation continues, and Mahoning County prosecutors will decide how the case proceeds. A motive has not been established.

An armed man barreled through a crowd toward Democratic Ohio gubernatorial candidate Amy Acton on Sunday, knocking people down before her security detail stopped him, authorities say.
The incident unfolded around 2:30 p.m. at the Mahoning County Democratic Party tent at the Canfield Fair, where Acton was speaking to supporters.
Authorities identified the man as Patrick Havas, 38, of Canfield.
According to the Mahoning County Sheriff’s Office, Havas entered the tent holding up a cellphone as though he were recording the event before he began aggressively pushing his way through the crowd.
Witnesses described a chaotic scene.
Former Democratic Rep. John Boccieri, who was there, told The Washington Post that the man “barreled” through the gathering, knocking an elderly man and woman to the ground as he moved toward Acton.
CBS News reported that one of the people knocked over was an older man with Parkinson’s disease who hit his head after falling. Then Acton’s security detail intervened.
Ohio State Highway Patrol troopers confronted Havas before he reached the candidate, and Canfield Fair police took him into custody.
What police found on him immediately raised the stakes.
Authorities say Havas was carrying two handguns and brass knuckles. The Ohio State Highway Patrol said he also possessed a Taser.
But authorities emphasized an important distinction: None of the weapons was brandished or removed from its holster during the incident.
Acton was not injured.
Her campaign initially described Havas as an “armed individual” who “lunged” at the candidate and injured multiple people.
Acton remained at the fair afterward and was photographed helping tend to one of the people who had been knocked down.
Havas was taken to the Mahoning County Jail and booked on two counts of assault and one count of disorderly conduct.
Investigators have not publicly established his motive.
Mahoning County Democratic Party Chairman Chris Anderson urged people not to jump to conclusions about why Havas was there. “I don’t know why he was there — that’s for law enforcement to discover,” Anderson said.
Republicans quickly joined Democrats in condemning the incident.
Ohio Gov. Mike DeWine said he spoke with Acton afterward and confirmed she was OK. “Violence or the threat of violence at political or public events is always unacceptable,” DeWine said.
Acton’s Republican opponent, Vivek Ramaswamy, issued an unequivocal condemnation through his campaign. “Candidates should be able to meet with voters without having to worry about threats or violence,” Ramaswamy communications director Connie Luck said. “What happened today is completely unacceptable and has no place in politics.”
Republican Sen. Jon Husted similarly said there was “no place for this kind of behavior.”
The incident comes with less than two months remaining in one of the country’s most closely watched gubernatorial races. Acton, Ohio’s former health director who became nationally known during the COVID pandemic, is facing Ramaswamy in November.
For now, however, the political implications take a back seat to what investigators still need to determine: Why an armed man forced his way through a crowd toward a candidate for governor in the first place.

Havas was booked on two assault charges and one disorderly-conduct charge. Authorities had not publicly established his motive, and it was not immediately clear whether he had an attorney. Any conclusion about why he approached Acton, whether he intended to use the weapons, or how much preparation preceded the incident would therefore go beyond the information investigators had released.

The confrontation took place at the Mahoning County Democratic Party tent, one of the open settings that make county fairs valuable campaign stops. Candidates can speak directly with voters there, but the same proximity that makes those appearances useful also makes controlling access difficult.
Contrary to the initial suggestion that Acton may have been relying only on the fair’s general police presence, she already had a dedicated law-enforcement detail. Local reporting based on the sheriff’s office account says her security detail consisted of Ohio State Highway Patrol troopers. Those troopers confronted Havas as he pushed through the crowd, and Canfield Fair police officers then took him into custody.
That distinction matters. The incident did not occur because Acton arrived without protection. It occurred despite the presence of trained officers, illustrating how quickly a confrontation can develop when a candidate appears in a dense public crowd.

Protests were held outside her home after she became one of the most visible officials associated with the state’s public-health restrictions. Acton left the fair unharmed because officers were already present and responded quickly. The unresolved question is not whether she had protection, but how public campaigning remains genuinely public when even a staffed security detail cannot prevent every armed person from entering the crowd.
